title: We Wear Away, but the Rising Stars Do Not
intro: Labid mourns his maternal half-brother Arbad ibn Qays. The stars still rise and the reservoirs outlast their builders, but the neighbour who once sheltered him is gone. Imagining his own old age, Labid pictures fingers hooked about a staff and a worn scabbard with a good blade inside. The manuscripts differ over where the elegy ends. Al-Nahari recites twenty verses, including the challenge to foretell a death or a fall of rain.

translation: We wear away, while the rising stars endure
and mountains and reservoirs outlast us.
1.sharh: The stars come round again. Even the reservoirs people build can outlast the hands that made them. The comparison gives the loss of one man a scale larger than a lifetime.

translation: I once lived under a cherished protector’s wing.
In Arbad I have lost a neighbour who stood by me.
2.sharh: A neighbour in this sense is someone whose protection one can claim. Only in the second half does Labid give the lost protector his brother’s name.

translation: I will not lose heart if time parts us.
One day time bereaves every man.
3.sharh: His composure costs him something. He has just named the man he needs, and now reminds himself that everyone who loves someone takes a turn at mourning.

translation: No new gain comes to me with joy,
nor do I despair at what time has done.
4.sharh: A windfall and a bereavement pull in opposite directions. He measures the steadiness he claims for himself against both.

translation: People are like the dwellings they inhabit,
full the day they settle, empty by morning.
5.sharh: A campsite can be full of people one evening and bare ground the next day. That abrupt change is how a whole human life looks from a distance.

translation: A man is only a flame and its light.
It turns to ash after flaring bright.
6.sharh: A burning brand lights up the ground around it. Ash is what the thing that gave that light becomes.

translation: Goodness is the piety kept within.
Wealth is a loan for life, a trust.
7.sharh: The inward disposition belongs to the doer. For property Labid borrows the language of a lifetime grant, whose use can last many years and still come to an end.

translation: Wealth and family are only a deposit,
and one day deposits must be returned.
8.sharh: Family now enters the same reckoning as wealth. Calling both a single deposit makes the death of someone close feel like a claim falling due.

translation: They go in companies, and you are left behind them,
as a herdsman gathers the last of the stragglers.
9.sharh: People leave in droves. To be at the rear offers only a little time, as the man following a herd makes sure the last animal comes along too.

translation: People do one of two kinds of work.
One wrecks what he builds, another raises it.
10.sharh: Both people work. The difference lies in whether a person’s later actions strengthen what the earlier ones accomplished or pull it down.

translation: One is fortunate and takes his share.
Another is wretched, content with a living.
11.sharh: The fortunate person lays claim to a share that will last. The other sets his sights no further than getting by, a small return on the life he spends.

translation: Does there not lie ahead, if my death is slow,
a stick with fingers bent around it?
12.sharh: There is a cost even to being spared. Labid lets a hand closing round a stick bring old age into view before showing the whole bent figure.

translation: I tell the stories of generations gone.
I creep along, bowed even when I stand.
13.sharh: The old man has become a living record of vanished people. While his listeners can travel back with him in a story, he can barely cross the ground himself.

translation: I have become a sword whose sheath is changed
by long years since the smith, its blade still keen.
14.sharh: Age marks the scabbard on the outside. A listener who judged the speaker by his bent back would overlook the edge still inside.

translation: May you never be far. Death has an appointment
with you. One nears the rise, another crests it.
15.sharh: “May you never be far” is an old farewell to the dead. The road rises ahead of everyone. The difference is how far along it each traveller has come.

translation: You who reproach me, what have you beyond a guess,
when the young men leave, of who will return?
16.sharh: He turns on the woman who chides him. An onlooker can see the young setting out together, but cannot pick out the one who will come home.

translation: She weeps over the youth that has gone.
Youth has its own companions, the young.
17.sharh: Her grief looks backward to his younger days. Youth itself is in company elsewhere, with a fresh generation growing up.

translation: Do you grieve at what time does to a man?
What generous man has escaped its blows?
18.sharh: Worth offers no exemption. By asking after the best people anyone can name, he makes a common lot bear some of the weight of his particular loss.

translation: By your life, women who cast pebbles cannot tell,
nor those who read birds, what God will do.
19.sharh: The diviners have signs one can watch and interpret, pebbles on the ground and birds in flight. Neither practice grants access to God’s decision.

translation: Ask them, if you think me false, when a man
will taste death, or when the rain will fall.
20.sharh: He proposes a test with answers anyone could check afterwards. A death and a rainfall matter intensely to the people waiting for them, and neither will keep a diviner’s appointment.

1.1.1.head: بَلِيَ
1.1.1.meaning: To wear out through age, as cloth does. Here the wear is on human lives.

1.2.4.head: المَصانِع
1.2.4.meaning: Built reservoirs that hold water. Another early gloss gives fortified buildings.

2.1.4.head: أَكناف
2.1.4.meaning: The sheltering sides of something. To live in someone’s shelter is to enjoy their protection.

2.1.5-6.head: جار مَضِنَّة
2.1.5-6.meaning: “A neighbour one would begrudge losing”, someone whose protection is especially dear.

2.2.3.head: أَربَد
2.2.3.meaning: Arbad ibn Qays, Labid’s maternal half-brother and the subject of the elegy.

3.1.2.head: جَزِع
3.1.2.meaning: Someone who loses composure under grief.

3.2.6.head: فاجِع
3.2.6.meaning: One who bereaves another of someone dear.

4.1.4.head: طَريف
4.1.4.meaning: A newly acquired possession, as distinct from inherited property. An early alternative takes Tarif as a man’s name.

5.2.3.head: حَلَّ
5.2.3.meaning: To settle at a place or pitch camp there.

6.1.4.head: الشِّهاب
6.1.4.meaning: A flame or firebrand. The ash in the next half points to a fire burning out.

6.2.1.head: حارَ
6.2.1.meaning: To turn back or change into something else.

7.1.4.head: مُضمَرات
7.1.4.meaning: Things held within, here a person’s inward intentions.

7.2.4.head: مُعمَرات
7.2.4.meaning: Lifetime grants, property given for use over the course of a life.

8.1.5.head: وَديعَة
8.1.5.meaning: Something entrusted to another for safekeeping until its return.

9.1.3.head: خَلَفَ
9.1.3.meaning: You are left behind as they depart. The recitation addresses the hearer, where the diwan reads “we are left”.

9.2.5.head: المُشايِع
9.2.5.meaning: The herdsman bringing up the rear and gathering in the stragglers.

10.2.1.head: تَبَّرَ
10.2.1.meaning: To break up or bring to ruin.

11.2.4.head: قانِع
11.2.4.meaning: Content with what supplies a living, and seeking no further good here.

12.1.4-5.meaning: “My appointed death held back”, meaning that he is granted still more years.

12.2.3.head: حَنى
12.2.3.meaning: To be bent or folded, as fingers close round a stick.

13.1.3.head: القُرون
13.1.3.meaning: Generations, the people who lived before the speaker.

13.2.1.head: دَبَّ
13.2.1.meaning: To creep or advance in short, slow steps.

14.1.5.head: جَفن
14.1.5.meaning: A scabbard, the covering around a blade.

14.2.3.head: القَين
14.2.3.meaning: A craftsman, here the smith who made the sword.

15.1.1-2.head: لا تَبعَدَنَّ
15.1.1-2.meaning: “May you never be far”, a traditional farewell addressed to the dead.

15.2.2.head: دانٍ
15.2.2.meaning: Drawing near. The climb ahead stands for the approach of death.

16.1.1.head: عاذِلَة
16.1.1.meaning: A shortened call to the woman who reproaches him.

16.1.5.head: تَظَنٍّ
16.1.5.meaning: Conjecture, a guess about what no observer can know.

17.2.5.head: الرَّعارِع
17.2.5.meaning: Young people who have grown past childhood.

18.2.5.head: القَوارِع
18.2.5.meaning: Disasters imagined as blows striking a person.

19.1.4-5.head: الضَّرب بِالحَصى
19.1.4-5.meaning: “Casting pebbles”, a form of divination using small stones.

19.2.2-3.head: زَجر الطَّير
19.2.2-3.meaning: “Reading the birds”, drawing omens from their flight or direction.

20.2.2.meaning: Appointed deaths, the end allotted to each life.

20.2.5.head: الغَيث
20.2.5.meaning: Rain coming to the relief of dry country.
